content: Speech communication involves the processes related to the production and perception of sounds utilized in spoken language. Various academic disciplines, such as acoustics, psychology, speech pathology, linguistics, and computer science, study speech and the sounds associated with it. In the field of linguistics, particularly articulatory phonetics, the manner of articulation describes how the tongue, lips, and other speech organs interact to produce specific sounds. This concept is often applied to the production of consonants. For any given place of articulation, there can be multiple manners of articulation, resulting in several homorganic consonants. Speech perception refers to the processes by which humans interpret and understand the sounds used in language. The study of speech perception is closely tied to the fields of phonetics and phonology in linguistics, as well as cognitive psychology and perceptual psychology. Research in this area aims to understand how human listeners recognize speech sounds and use this information to comprehend spoken language. This research has practical applications, such as developing computer systems capable of recognizing speech and improving speech recognition for individuals with hearing or language impairments. Several biological and psychological factors can affect speech. These include: Diseases and disorders of the lungs or vocal cords, such as paralysis, respiratory infections, vocal fold nodules, and cancers of the lungs and throat. Neurological conditions affecting the brain, such as alogia, aphasias, dysarthria, dystonia, and speech processing disorders. These conditions may impair motor planning, nerve transmission, phonological processing, or the perception of the intended message, leading to difficulties in speech production. Hearing problems, such as otitis media with effusion, which can result in phonological issues. Articulatory problems, including stuttering, lisping, cleft palate, ataxia, or nerve damage, which can interfere with the ability to articulate sounds properly. Tourette syndrome and tics can also impact speech. Beyond aphasias, conditions like anomia and certain types of dyslexia can hinder auditory perception and, consequently, expression. Hearing impairments and deafness also fall into this category, as they can significantly affect speech and communication.
